---
title: "What does it look like?"
---


A three-view of the airframe, and the three dimensions that fix its size.

::: {#f519ebaf .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
wing, stab, fin = mceagle.wings
l_fus_m = mceagle.fuselages[0].length()
```
:::


**Answer.** A shoulder-wing glider spanning
29\.2 cm as built, on a
43\.8 cm fuselage plate, with
13\.3° of dihedral (@fig-three-view).

The span above is the finished glider, tip to tip. The flat pattern you cut is
wider, because bending the tips up shortens the projected span — a distinction
the cutting entry depends on, and the one dimension of this aircraft most easily
got wrong. Everything here is read back off the `Airplane` object rather than
recomputed from the tables that built it, so it is the geometry `AeroBuildup`
actually sees.

::: {#cell-fig-three-view .cell fig-height='7' fig-width='7' execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
# Bind the returned axes -- otherwise their repr renders as a second output and
# demotes the figure to a subfigure.
_ = mceagle.draw_three_view(show=True)
```
